issues.legal_issue: The contractual period for offering apartment possession runs from the date the required fire-safety approval is obtained when that approval is a precondition to construction.
material_facts: The agreement calculated the possession period from approval of the building plans and/or fulfilment of preconditions imposed under them.
The applicable fire-safety requirement, the sanctioned plans and the environmental clearance required fire-safety approval before construction began.
The developer obtained the fire-safety approval after delays, and construction had begun before that approval was obtained.
issues.conclusion: The contractual possession period, including the grace period, was to be computed from the date the fire-safety approval was granted, rather than from the date the building plans were sanctioned.
issues.legal_principle: Clause 13.3 of the Apartment Buyer’s Agreement linked the possession period to approval of the building plans and/or fulfilment of their preconditions. Section 15 of the Haryana Fire Safety Act, 2009 required fire-safety approval before construction, and the sanctioned plans and environmental clearance imposed the same requirement. The Court therefore treated the fire approval as the relevant precondition. It also found that the developer had taken approximately seven months to obtain it.

predicates.housing_possession_dispute: A buyer and a developer disputed when the contractual period for offering possession of a housing unit began.
predicates.contract_links_possession_period_to_plan: The developer and buyer agreed that the possession period would run from building-plan approval or fulfilment of preconditions imposed under the plans.
predicates.fire_safety_approval_required_before_con: The applicable requirements made fire-safety approval a precondition to commencing construction.

issues.definition: When a housing possession dispute concerns a contract tied to plan approval or its preconditions and fire-safety approval was required before construction, the possession period runs from that approval.

issues.legal_issue: Oppressive and one-sided terms in a housing buyer agreement may constitute an unfair trade practice, and consumer fora may decline to enforce those terms under the earlier consumer-protection regime.
material_facts: The agreement required buyers to pay substantial amounts early and imposed a high rate of interest for late payments.
It offered the developer only modest delay compensation, restricted the buyer’s right to terminate and obtain a refund, and allowed the developer to forfeit earnest money and make other deductions.
The agreement also delayed refunds until resale of the apartment and treated possession as a waiver of claims against the developer.
The buyers had little practical choice but to accept the developer-drafted agreement.
issues.conclusion: The agreement contained oppressive, wholly one-sided terms constituting an unfair trade practice, and the developer could not compel the buyers to be bound by them.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 2(1)(c), 2(1)(g), 2(1)(o) and 2(1)(r) of the Consumer Protection Act, 1986 cover complaints about unfair trade practices, deficiency in service and housing construction services. Section 14 empowers consumer fora to redress deficiencies and discontinue unfair or restrictive trade practices. The Court relied on Lucknow Development Authority v. M.K. Gupta, Fortune Infrastructure v. Trevor D’Lima, Pioneer Urban Land and Infrastructure Ltd. v. Govindan Raghavan, and Wg. Cdr. Arifur Rahman Khan v. DLF Southern Homes Pvt. Ltd. It held that the earlier Act implicitly empowered consumer fora to address unfair contractual terms, notwithstanding the later Act’s express provision concerning unfair contracts.

predicates.housing_consumer_dispute: A buyer brought a consumer proceeding concerning a developer’s housing-construction service.
predicates.developer_drafted_terms_are_oppressive_o: The developer’s agreement placed materially harsher obligations on the buyer than on the developer, including in relation to delay, termination or refund.
predicates.buyer_had_no_real_choice_to_negotiate: The buyer had no practical choice but to accept the developer-prepared agreement.

issues.definition: If a buyer brings a housing consumer dispute over oppressive developer-drafted terms that the buyer had no real choice to negotiate, the consumer forum may decline to enforce those terms.

issues.legal_issue: The availability of remedies under real-estate legislation does not displace the consumer-protection remedy, although a complainant may not pursue both remedies simultaneously for the same cause of action.
material_facts: Buyers pursued complaints before consumer fora concerning delay and deficiency in housing services.
A buyer in the same project also obtained a decision from the real-estate authority concerning possession and interest.
The developer argued that the real-estate authority’s decision should take precedence over the consumer forum’s jurisdiction.
issues.conclusion: The consumer-protection remedy remained available alongside remedies under the real-estate legislation; the allottee could choose a remedy but could not simultaneously pursue both for the same cause of action.
issues.legal_principle: Section 3 of the Consumer Protection Act, 1986 and Sections 18 and 88 of the Real Estate (Regulation and Development) Act, 2016 preserve additional remedies. Section 79 of the latter Act bars civil-court jurisdiction, not proceedings before consumer fora. The proviso to Section 71 gives a complainant an option to withdraw a pending consumer complaint and proceed before the real-estate adjudicating officer. The Court relied on Secretary, Thirumurugan Cooperative Agricultural Credit Society v. M. Lalitha, National Seeds Corporation Ltd. v. M. Madhusudhan Reddy, Emaar MGF Land Ltd. v. Aftab Singh and M/s Imperia Structures Ltd. v. Anil Patni. It also applied the doctrine of election, discussed in A.P. State Financial Corporation v. GAR Re-rolling Corporation, National Insurance Co. Ltd. v. Mastan and Transcore v. Union of India.

predicates.housing_consumer_proceeding: A buyer brought a consumer proceeding about a housing service or a developer’s failure to perform its obligations.
predicates.real_estate_law_preserves_other_remedies: The applicable real-estate framework leaves remedies under other laws available in addition to its own remedies.
predicates.jurisdictional_bar_is_limited_to_civil_c: The real-estate framework bars civil-court proceedings on matters entrusted to its authorities but does not bar proceedings before consumer fora.
predicates.complainant_does_not_pursue_both_remedie: The complainant selects one available remedy rather than pursuing both remedies at the same time for the same cause of action.

issues.definition: When a buyer brings a housing consumer proceeding, other remedies are preserved, the jurisdictional bar is confined to civil courts, and the buyer does not pursue both remedies simultaneously, the consumer remedy remains available as an alternative.

issues.legal_issue: Buyers whose completed apartments have an occupation certificate and for whom possession has been offered must accept possession, while remaining entitled to compensation for the delay.
material_facts: The relevant apartments were in completed towers for which an occupation certificate had been issued.
The developer offered possession of those apartments after obtaining the certificate.
The offers came after the contractual deadline for possession.
issues.conclusion: The buyers in the completed towers were obligated to take possession, and the developer was obligated to pay delay compensation for the period between the contractual deadline and the offer of possession.
issues.legal_principle: Clause 13.4 of the Apartment Buyer’s Agreement provided for delay compensation after the grace period. The Court applied that provision to the completed units for which occupation certificates had been issued and possession had been offered, while rejecting the buyers’ entitlement to refuse those completed apartments.

predicates.housing_possession_consumer_appeal: A consumer appeal concerns a buyer’s claim arising from delayed possession of a housing unit.
predicates.occupation_certificate_obtained: The relevant unit was in a completed building for which an occupation certificate had been issued.
predicates.possession_offered_for_completed_unit: The developer offered possession of the completed unit to the buyer.

issues.definition: When an occupation certificate has been obtained and possession of the completed unit has been offered in a housing-possession consumer appeal, the buyer must accept possession and is entitled to delay compensation.

issues.legal_issue: Buyers whose apartments remain incomplete without occupation certificates after substantial delay may obtain a refund with interest without forfeiture or other deductions.
material_facts: The buyers’ allotted towers lacked occupation certificates and the apartments were not ready for possession even by the date set by the real-estate authority.
The buyers had paid part of the consideration and observed that construction was not progressing, after which they stopped paying further instalments and sought refunds.
The developer had offered alternative units in completed towers, but the buyers did not accept them.
The developer had itself contributed to the delay, including by taking approximately seven months to obtain the fire-safety approval.
issues.conclusion: The buyers in the incomplete towers were entitled to a refund of the entire amount they had deposited with simple interest. The developer could not deduct earnest money or other amounts under the agreement.
issues.legal_principle: The Court relied on the consumer’s right to seek a refund for inordinate delay and deficiency in service, including the principles in Fortune Infrastructure v. Trevor D’Lima and Pioneer Urban Land and Infrastructure Ltd. v. Govindan Raghavan. The delay-compensation term in Clause 13.4 was inadequate, and the agreement’s forfeiture and deduction terms could not be enforced in light of the developer’s defaults and the one-sided nature of the agreement. The Court set a fair interest remedy after considering the parties’ competing interests and prevailing market conditions.

rule.if: housing_possession_consumer_appeal and substantial_possession_delay and occupation_certificate_not_obtained and apartment_not_ready_for_possession

predicates.housing_possession_consumer_appeal: A consumer appeal concerns a buyer’s claim arising from delayed possession of a housing unit.
predicates.substantial_possession_delay: The developer failed to complete and offer possession within the applicable contractual period and the delay was substantial.
predicates.occupation_certificate_not_obtained: No occupation certificate had been obtained for the building containing the buyer’s allotted unit.
predicates.apartment_not_ready_for_possession: The allotted apartment was still not ready for possession.

issues.definition: When a buyer in a housing-possession consumer appeal faces substantial delay and the allotted apartment remains unready without an occupation certificate, the buyer is entitled to a full refund with interest and without deductions.

issues.legal_issue: A developer that undertakes to refund a buyer’s principal amount but fails to do so may be directed to make that refund with interest.
material_facts: The developer filed an affidavit in a proceeding before an insolvency tribunal offering to repay the buyer’s principal amount in instalments.
The developer did not make the promised repayment.
The buyer sought relief in the ensuing appeal.
issues.conclusion: The developer was directed to refund the deposited amount with interest, with a higher default rate applying if it failed to comply with the direction.
issues.legal_principle: The Court relied on the developer’s recorded undertaking to refund the principal amount and its failure to honour that undertaking. No earlier case was cited as the basis for this case-specific direction.

predicates.housing_buyer_appeal: An appeal concerns a buyer’s dispute with a housing developer.
predicates.developer_undertook_to_refund_principal: The developer formally offered to refund the buyer’s principal amount.
predicates.developer_failed_to_honour_refund_undert: The developer did not make the refund it had formally offered.

issues.definition: If a developer formally undertakes to refund a housing buyer’s principal amount but fails to do so, the developer must refund it with interest.
